    Yes, switching to Mac is simple, and learning how to use Mac feels just as easy as using your iPhone. Mac pairs seamlessly with your iPhone and other Apple devices.
    
    If you already have an iPhone, setting up your Mac is a snap. Just bring your iPhone near your Mac, and Setup Assistant signs you in to your Wi-Fi network and Apple Account. Your files, photos, messages, passwords, and more are transferred from iCloud right to your new Mac.
    
    Don’t have an iPhone? No problem. With Migration Assistant preinstalled on every Mac, you can easily transfer your documents, apps, accounts, and settings from a PC or an existing Mac. Once the transfer is complete, everything will be ready on your new Mac.
    
    Need more help? With Personal Setup, you get free online, one-on-one sessions with a Specialist who walks you through setup and shows you how to make the most of your new Mac. Best of all, you can join whenever works for you, from wherever you are.
    
*   ### Does Apple offer any special discounts or promotions to higher education students, parents, and teachers?
    
    Apple has an Education Store dedicated to your needs. You’ll find discounts, promotions, and bundle deals on Mac, iPad, software, and accessories. You can also access tools and resources to learn how you can better use your Apple devices, software, and apps to enhance learning and teaching.
    
    Products eligible for education discounts are marked with a graduation cap icon. You may need to verify your eligibility with an active school email or other documentation during checkout. Verification varies by country.
    
    [Shop the Education Store (Opens in a new window)](https://www.apple.com/us-edu/store)
    
*   ### What’s the fastest way to get my order, and what are my delivery options?
    
    If you need a Mac right away, visit your local Apple Store to check in-stock availability and options for same-day pickup. In most metro areas, we offer same-day scheduled courier delivery on available in-stock items from an Apple Store. The two-hour delivery fee is $9. You’ll choose a delivery date and time during checkout. Subject to availability. Delivery options, which you can select during checkout, depend on your location and the product availability. While many Mac configurations are ready to ship or pick up in a store, some customized selections may impact your delivery estimates and options.
    
    Orders placed on apple.com can only be shipped within the country or region of purchase. Visit the online store of the location where you want your products delivered.
    
*   ### Can I connect my Mac to additional displays?
    
    Yes. The number of additional displays that can be connected will depend on your Mac model and chip, and could also vary depending on display resolution.
    
    Get more details about connecting to external displays for each Mac model:
    
    *   [MacBook Neo](https://support.apple.com/en-us/126473)
        
    *   [MacBook Air](https://support.apple.com/en-us/122212)
        
    *   [MacBook Pro](https://support.apple.com/en-us/101571)
        
    *   [iMac](https://support.apple.com/guide/imac/connect-a-display-apd271f29cb9/mac)
        
    *   [Mac mini](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102194)
        
    *   [Mac Studio](https://support.apple.com/en-us/101910)
        
    
*   ### What are my payment and financing options?
    
    Apple accepts Apple Pay, most credit and debit cards, PayPal, Apple Gift Cards, and Apple Card. You can also split your payment across multiple cards as long as they share the same billing address.
    
    When you choose to check out at Apple with Apple Card Monthly Installments, you can pay for your new device over time, interest-free, Footnote ◊ and you’ll receive 3% Daily Cash back up front.
    
    If you don’t have Apple Card yet, you can apply for one in as little as a minute when you select Apple Card Monthly Installments as your payment option and use it for your purchase.
    
    [Learn more about Apple Card Monthly Installments(Opens in a new window)](https://www.apple.com/apple-card/monthly-installments)
    
    If you used your Apple Card to pay in full, but you meant to take advantage of interest-free financing using Apple Card Monthly Installments, we can help you get switched over. Contact an Apple Card Specialist at 877-255-5923. You can also chat with one by tapping Apple Card in Wallet, tapping the More button in the upper-right corner, and then tapping Message.
    
*   ### How does Apple Trade In work?
    
    Apple Trade In makes it easy to get credit toward the purchase of your new Mac. Just answer a few questions about your device and its condition. Based on what you tell us, we’ll provide an estimated trade-in value. Footnote ∆ If you buy online and choose to pay with Apple Card Monthly Installments, we’ll apply the value as an instant credit to lower the monthly payments of your new device. If you pay in full, we’ll credit your payment method after we receive your trade-in. And if it’s not eligible for credit, we’ll provide a simple way to recycle it for free.
    
    If it’s eligible for trade-in, we’ll mail you a free trade-in kit. You may receive it along with your new device. Otherwise it will be mailed to you separately as soon as your order is ready for delivery or pickup. Once you receive the trade-in kit, you have 14 days to prepare and send in your device.
    
    Once we receive your trade-in, we'll inspect it and verify its condition. If everything checks out, there’s nothing more you need to do. If your device doesn’t match the condition you described, you’ll receive an email with next steps.
    
    If you paid in full and the value of your device was more than the cost of your new Mac, you’ll receive an Apple Gift Card by email with the remaining amount.
    
    The online trade-in process can take up to 2 to 3 weeks. You can also trade in your device at an Apple Store at the point of purchase. However, the trade-in value in-store may be different from the estimated trade-in value you received online.
    
*   ### What protection does AppleCare offer?
    
    AppleCare+ extends the standard warranty for your new Mac. It provides unlimited repairs for accidents like drops and spills, as well as battery replacements at no extra charge. You’ll also get access to 24/7 priority support from Apple experts. Footnote §
    
    If you choose AppleCare One, you get all the same benefits of AppleCare+ for up to three devices, plus theft and loss coverage for iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. Footnote ±
    
    If you have an active AppleCare+ plan, you can still upgrade to an AppleCare One plan. Other eligible devices are those currently associated with your Apple Account, Apple audio or headphones less than one year old, and other Apple devices that are less than four years old and in good condition. When you switch plans, we’ll automatically cancel your current one and refund any amount owed.
    
    [Learn more about AppleCare+ (Opens in a new window)](https://www.apple.com/applecare)
    
*   ### Can I return or exchange my Mac?
    
    If you change your mind and no longer wish to keep your Mac, you have the option to return it or exchange it. The returned device must be in good condition and in the original packaging, including all accessories, manuals, and instructions. Returns are subject to Apple’s Sales and Refunds Policy.
    
    [Learn more about returns, refunds, and exchanges(Opens in a new window)](https://www.apple.com/shop/help/returns_refund)

Apple Mac Studio 2025 (M3 Ultra 32-core / 80-core GPU / 512GB RAM / 4TB SSD)
============================================================================

Manufacturer: **Apple**

The Apple Mac Studio 2025, configured with the M3 Ultra processor, represents the high end of Apple's compact desktop lineup. Built around a 32-core CPU running at up to 3.7 GHz across its performance cores, this configuration pairs that processing headroom with **512GB of unified RAM** — the maximum supported by this platform — alongside a 4TB NVMe SSD. The machine weighs 3,640 g and occupies a footprint of 196 × 196 mm with a height of 94 mm.

On the graphics side, the integrated 80-core GPU supports up to eight simultaneous displays and delivers a **maximum memory bandwidth of 819 GB/s** over a PCIe 4 interface, with the GPU fabricated on a 3 nm process node. Connectivity includes two USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports, four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C ports, one HDMI output, one RJ45 Ethernet port, a 3.5 mm audio jack, Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax), and Bluetooth 5.3. Benchmark results show a Geekbench 6 multi-core score of 27,749 and a single-core score of 3,221. The CPU carries an 80W TDP, uses a hybrid big.LITTLE core arrangement with HMP scheduling, and does not support simultaneous multithreading.

Pros

*   The 32-core CPU with 24 cores at 3.7 GHz and 8 at 3.4 GHz, combined with 512GB of DDR5 unified memory, provides substantial headroom for heavily threaded desktop workloads
*   Support for up to eight simultaneous displays makes this machine well-suited for multi-monitor desktop setups
*   A maximum memory bandwidth of 819 GB/s from the integrated 80-core GPU enables rapid data throughput for graphics-intensive tasks
*   The 4TB NVMe SSD delivers fast storage access in a form factor measuring just 196 x 196 x 94 mm
*   Wi-Fi 6E support alongside Bluetooth 5.3 covers both high-bandwidth wireless networking and modern peripheral connectivity
*   Hardware security features including TrustZone and NX bit support are built directly into the processor

Cons

*   No Thunderbolt 3 or Thunderbolt 4 ports are included, limiting compatibility with certain high-speed peripherals and docks that rely on those interfaces
*   There are no DisplayPort or USB 4 outputs, which restricts options for connecting some monitors and high-speed external devices
*   ECC memory is not supported, which may be a consideration for workloads where memory error correction is a requirement
*   The absence of S/PDIF output limits legacy professional audio routing options for users who depend on that interface
*   With no USB 2.0 or USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports available, older USB peripherals must rely on adapters to connect to the available Gen 2 ports

##### Who is this for?

This machine is well-matched to users who run **heavily threaded desktop workloads** that can take full advantage of a 32-core CPU and 512GB of DDR5 unified memory — such as large-scale data processing, complex computational tasks, or multi-stream media work. The integrated 80-core GPU with 819 GB/s memory bandwidth and support for **up to eight simultaneous displays** also makes it a strong fit for professionals managing extensive multi-monitor setups or driving high-resolution visual output across multiple screens. The compact 196 × 196 × 94 mm chassis paired with Wi-Fi 6E and a broad USB 3.2 Gen 2 port selection suits users who need a capable desktop workstation without sacrificing desk space.

##### Who is this NOT for?

Users who depend on **Thunderbolt 3 or Thunderbolt 4 connectivity** for high-speed external storage arrays, professional docks, or specialized peripherals will find the absence of those ports a meaningful limitation. Similarly, workflows that require **ECC memory** for error-corrected computation — common in certain scientific, financial, or mission-critical server-adjacent tasks — are not supported by this platform. Those who need DisplayPort outputs or USB 4 connections for specific display or device configurations will also encounter compatibility gaps without additional adapters.

The M3 Ultra's CPU is configured with **32 cores running across two clock speed tiers** — 24 cores at 3.7 GHz and 8 cores at 3.4 GHz — yielding 32 threads in total, though without simultaneous multithreading. It operates within an 80W TDP envelope, supports 64-bit computing, and includes integrated graphics. The processor also carries **32 MB of L2 cache**, and uses a heterogeneous core arrangement consistent with its big.LITTLE-style design.

The Mac Studio 2025 offers a well-rounded set of wired and wireless connectivity options. On the wireless side, it supports **Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax)** alongside Wi-Fi 6, Wi-Fi 5, and Wi-Fi 4, and includes Bluetooth 5.3. Wired connections consist of two USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports and **four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C ports**, along with one HDMI output, one RJ45 Ethernet port, and a 3.5 mm audio jack. There are no USB 2.0, USB 3.2 Gen 1, USB 4, Thunderbolt 3 or 4, DisplayPort, VGA, or S/PDIF ports included.

Classified as a desktop CPU, the M3 Ultra in the Mac Studio 2025 employs **big.LITTLE technology with Heterogeneous Multi-Processing (HMP)**, allowing the system to schedule tasks across its performance and efficiency cores simultaneously. The processor includes an NX bit and TrustZone support, contributing to its hardware-level security capabilities. Maximum supported memory tops out at 512GB, and while the platform does not support ECC memory, that ceiling aligns with the unified memory configuration available in this model.

##### Final Verdict

The Apple Mac Studio 2025 (M3 Ultra) is a compact desktop workstation built around an exceptionally high specification floor — 32 CPU cores, **512GB of DDR5 unified memory with 819 GB/s bandwidth**, a 4TB NVMe SSD, and support for up to eight simultaneous displays, all within a chassis barely larger than a hardback book. Its hardware security features, Wi-Fi 6E, and broad USB 3.2 Gen 2 port selection round out a well-considered feature set for stationary professional use. The absence of Thunderbolt and ECC memory support will matter to a specific subset of users, but for those whose workflows align with what this machine offers, it represents a highly capable and space-efficient desktop platform.

 [![Avatar for Zac Hall](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/af01c840dac8281fd5f1986a8504e54222700437fa19c3083e578c1ddf6386a6?s=60&d=mm&r=r)](https://9to5mac.com/author/apollozac/)

A year ago today, Apple unveiled the M4 Max and M3 Ultra Mac Studio desktop computer. In addition to Thunderbolt 5 and SSD storage configurable to 16TB, Apple advertised the Mac Studio as featuring up to 512GB of unified memory. As of this week, the highest RAM upgrade option is no longer available.

Apple [highlighted](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/03/apple-unveils-new-mac-studio-the-most-powerful-mac-ever/)
 the highest RAM configuration in the press release for the M3 Ultra Mac Studio:

> Mac Studio is a powerhouse for AI, capable of running large language models (LLMs) with over 600 billion parameters entirely in memory, thanks to its advanced GPU and up to 512GB of unified memory with M3 Ultra — the most ever in a personal computer.

As [MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/03/05/mac-studio-no-512gb-ram-upgrade/)
 notes, customers ordering a new M3 Ultra Mac Studio today no longer have the option to configure the desktop Mac with 512GB RAM. The issue is likely due to global supply constraints thanks in large part to high memory needs for servers powering AI.

The M3 Ultra Mac Studio still offers the most configurable RAM in a Mac with its 256GB memory option. That’s compared to the M2 Ultra Mac Pro which offers up to 192GB RAM, and M4 Max/M5 Max machines that support up to 128GB RAM.

### The Bottom Line

The M3 Ultra-equipped Apple Mac Studio delivers the massive multi-core performance and workstation grunt that pros with demanding workflows need. However, its high price and older core architecture mean the M4 Max model is more versatile—and accessible.

Pros & Cons
-----------

*   M3 Ultra delivers unparalleled performance for specific workflows
*   Massive memory and storage capacity
*   Enhanced connectivity, with six Thunderbolt 5 ports

*   Prohibitively expensive for casual use, especially in top configurations
*   Newer, cheaper M4 Max is better than M3 Ultra in some cases
*   No Wi-Fi 7

More Specs

The M3 Ultra version of the Mac Studio (starts at $3,999; $8,099 as tested) is the apex of Apple computers, capable of everything from editing 8K video and rendering complex CGI to running massive AI models on your own machine. From media editing to engineering, the Mac Studio is Apple's contender for the most powerful [workstation desktop](https://www.pcmag.com/picks/the-best-desktop-workstations)
 you can buy. (Even the tower-style Mac Pro is little more than a Mac Studio in a larger box.)

The 2025 Mac Studio has two essential versions, delineated by their CPU: the M4 Max and the M3 Ultra. Both are seriously powerful, and a meaningful upgrade over the previous models from 2023. However, the two processor offerings and slightly different feature sets may cause some confusion about which system is best for you and your work, not to mention your budget. That's why we've performed extensive testing on the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, to let you know when it's worth shelling out more for this more expensive and more powerful model. (Spoiler: The M3 Ultra model does offer top power for the most demanding tasks, but the [Mac Studio with M4 Max](https://www.pcmag.com/reviews/apple-mac-studio-2025-m4-max)
 gets our Editors’ Choice award over this one. Read on to learn why.)

**_Editor's Note (March 12, 2025):_** _This review was updated to include 3DMark graphics test results which were not available at the time of publishing. The overall rating has not changed._

Design: The M3 Ultra's Beastly Architecture
-------------------------------------------

The Mac Studio comes with your choice of two different processors: the single-chip M4 Max, which is the default for the base model, or the M3 Ultra, which costs an additional $2,000. The M3 Ultra, as the name suggests, is based upon the M3 Max, Apple's top-of-the-line single-chip [processor from 2023](https://www.pcmag.com/articles/apple-silicon-m3-cpus-tested-the-macs-most-advanced-chips-yet-compared)
.

![Apple Mac Studio (2025, M3 Ultra)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20768%20432'%3E%3Crect%20fill='%23f7f7f7'%20/%3E%3C/svg%3E)

(Credit: Brian Westover)

The M3 Ultra combines two M3 Max chips with Apple's proprietary UltraFusion silicon interposer, which bridges the two with an ultra-low latency connection, allowing the two chips to function and show up in software as one. The result is twice the compute cores, twice the bandwidth, a dramatic increase in the number of graphics cores, and support for more than half a terabyte of RAM.

First, a bit about the box it's in. On the outside, the Mac Studio looks quite familiar, since the external design is unchanged from the previous two iterations. One look at the pictures included in this review will tell you everything you need to know. The Mac Studio uses an all-aluminum construction for the cube-like chassis. This aluminum housing sits 3.7 inches tall and has a 7.7-inch square footprint, making it extremely compact and able to fit on any desk. The aluminum construction is more than just an aesthetic choice, though—it also functions as a heatsink for the hardware inside.

The Mac Studio is built for airflow, with a ring-shaped air intake on the bottom, circling the round foot that serves as the base of the Mac Studio. On the back side of the Studio, just above the rear ports, hundreds of little holes make up the exhaust ventilation. Inside the compact chassis is an extremely quiet fan that pulls cool air in and pushes hot air out, with a custom-designed heatsink dissipating heat from the processor. 

For this step-up model of the Mac Studio, a copper heatsink cools the processors, offering more effective cooling than the aluminum cooling block used in the base model. The change in material accounts for the near-2-pound difference between the M4 Max (6.1 pounds) and M3 Ultra models (8.0 pounds). Inside that heatsink is a vapor chamber for additional cooling efficiency.

The Mac Studio comes in several configurations, starting with a base model that uses the M4 Max 14-core processor with a 32-core GPU and 16-core neural engine. With a default allotment of 36GB of unified memory and 512GB of SSD storage, this version of the Mac Studio starts at $1,999. You can scale up the memory and storage as high as 128GB and 8TB, respectively, taking the price as high as $5,899.

Testing the 2025 Mac Studio: Evaluating the Monster M3 Ultra
------------------------------------------------------------

The Mac Studio is more than just a compact desktop; it's also a very powerful workstation machine, meaning that most desktops can't hold a candle to it. For this reason, we focused most of our comparisons on the most recent Mac Studio models, including the new [M4 Max model](https://www.pcmag.com/reviews/apple-mac-studio-2025-m4-max)
 and the [2023 Mac Studio with M2 Ultra](https://www.pcmag.com/reviews/apple-mac-studio-m2-ultra-2023)
. 

For some broader context, we've also compared it with the [Apple iMac with M4](https://www.pcmag.com/reviews/apple-imac-2024-m4)
. With no Pro, Max, or Ultra attached, that comparison illustrates just how far from mainstream the Mac Studio is in terms of performance and capability.

### Productivity and Content Creation Tests 

We run the same general productivity benchmarks across both mobile and desktop systems. For Macs, that means three benchmarks focus on the CPU, using all available cores and threads, to rate a PC's suitability for processor-intensive workloads. Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses the Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene, while Geekbench 6.3 Pro from Primate Labs simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning. Finally, we use the open-source video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute video clip from 4K to 1080p resolution (lower times are better).

We also run PugetBench for Photoshop by workstation maker Puget Systems. It works with the 2024 version of Adobe's famous image editor to rate a PC's performance for content creation and multimedia applications. It's an automated extension that executes a variety of general and GPU-accelerated Photoshop tasks ranging from opening, rotating, resizing, and saving an image to applying masks, gradient fills, and filters.

In Cinebench 2024, the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra led the pack by a giant margin, scoring more than 3,000 points—nearly 1,000 points more than the Mac Studio with M4 Max. And compared with something more pedestrian, like the Apple iMac, which uses a standard M4 processor, the difference in multicore processing performance is vast. However, if you look at single-core rendering performance, the M3 Ultra stops being so dominant. Because it uses M3 core technology, even the Apple iMac outpaced it in single-core performance.

We saw a similar split between multi-core and single-core performance in Geekbench Pro 6.3, where the M3 Ultra delivered category-leading scores in multi-core productivity testing but landed squarely in the middle of the pack for single-core performance due to the use of last-gen core technology.

Our Handbrake video transcoding test really drives home what that multi-core performance can do by showing how quickly the M3 Ultra's 32 processing cores can rip through a task. In this case, it converted our 12-minute 4K video file in 1 minute and 24 seconds. The M4 Max model took more than 2 minutes, while the M4 iMac took nearly 5. Even among high-performance systems, sub-2-minute times are rare, illustrating how quickly the raw power of the M3 Ultra can get through demanding tasks that are written to leverage all of its cores. 

Finally, you can see the difference between the M3 Ultra and the M4 Max in Adobe Photoshop, where the cheaper 16-core model delivered higher overall performance scores in photo editing and manipulation than the 32 cores of the M3 Ultra. It all highlights the fact that you need to choose the right processor for your use cases, with the cheaper M4 Max Mac Studio serving tasks like photo editing better.

### Graphics and Gaming Tests

Our Mac graphics and game testing starts with UL's 3DMark test suite, which uses the same animations and gaming simulations we use to test Windows machines.

Wild Life Extreme (4K) and Steel Nomad Light measure GPU speeds and gaming performance on Mac using Metal, Apple's proprietary graphics API, which is optimized for macOS and iOS devices. Steel Nomad Light's subtests also focus on gaming geometry and particle effects. 

We also use 3DMark's Solar Bay benchmark, which measures ray tracing performance in a synthetic environment. This benchmark works with Apple's Metal API and subjects 3D scenes to increasingly intense ray-traced workloads.

Finally, we use the built-in benchmark in Total War: Warhammer III for real-world gaming performance.

Despite the M3 Ultra's giant 80-core GPU, it wasn't the leader in our graphics tests. It usually took second place to the less expensive M4 Max and even fell short of other M4 chips—a testament to the GPU core enhancements introduced in the M4 series. As a result, the M3 Ultra fell behind in Wild Life Extreme and Solar Bay tests, though it produced the top score in Steel Nomad Light, leveraging those many GPU cores for exceptional performance with particle effects.

In our Warhammer III gaming tests, the M3 Ultra provided outstanding performance and better-than-playable frame rates at both Ultra and Low detail settings, indicating capable gaming performance. If you are in the unique class of gamers who are also Mac diehards and pro content creators, the M3 Ultra will definitely let you scratch that itch with support for the most demanding games you can get for Mac. 

But if you want the best gaming experience, the less-expensive M4 Max version of the Mac Studio is the better choice. In this same test, under the same settings, the M4 Max delivered higher frame rates and noticeably smoother gameplay at all detail settings. (Of course, gaming is a secondary concern on these machines; for the price of our tested M3 Ultra-based Mac Studio, you could buy a pile of gaming consoles and games likely taller than you are, plus a superb TV to play them on.)

### Workstation-Specific Tests 

The Mac Studio isn't just another desktop but a full-fledged workstation with the processing and graphics muscle to take on work in fields like engineering, medical imaging, and rendering CGI video. This level of performance demands some more thorough testing. To do that, we have a handful of workstation-tier tests, which include video editing in Adobe Premiere Pro 24, further editing in Blackmagic's DaVinci Resolve Studio, and rendering tests in Blender, targeting both CPU and GPU performance.

Each of these tests produces a numeric score. The fine distinctions between them aren't really important here, only the fact that a higher score means faster and more powerful performance.

In Adobe Premiere Pro, a professional-grade video editing program, the M3 Ultra really delivered on its promise of superior power, outperforming the M4 Max and showcasing its better suitability for professional-grade video editing workflows.

The M3 Ultra Mac Studio did the same in DaVinci Resolve, blazing past the M4 Max in video editing and color-correction tasks, proving that it's the processor of choice for professional editors.

Finally, in both CPU and GPU rendering tests in Blender, the M3 Ultra offered best-in-class performance, sticking the landing as the better choice for video work.

4.0

Excellent

If our tests showed anything, it's that the 2025 Apple Mac Studio with M3 Ultra has fantastically powerful processors that are perfect for the most demanding video and rendering tasks that an engineer or 3D animator can throw at it. But that doesn't make it the best choice for every user.

For tasks like photo editing and gaming, the updated core architecture of the M4 Max offers better and faster performance. But when raw power is needed in an application that can leverage all the cores it can get, the doubled-up M3 Ultra proves its worth. The individual cores may not be as powerful as those on the Mac Studio with M4 Max, but the sheer number of CPU and GPU cores will deliver top performance in the most demanding applications. 

If that's the sort of processing muscle you need for professional media work or mission-critical engineering and design, then the M3 Ultra is absolutely worth the extra expense. It's an investment that will pay off with faster project completion and smoother day-to-day work. But this does make the M3 Ultra Mac Studio more of a niche product than the M4 Max base configuration.

The end result? The 2025 Apple Mac Studio with M3 Ultra is a monster of a workstation that gets our recommendation for offices and studios that need unbridled power and are able to budget for it. (If you need this kind of multicore processing power, it's very likely that you know it.) For everyone else, the M4 Max configuration is the better Mac Studio and our top recommendation overall.

Mac Studio 512GB RAM Removed: Why Apple Pulled Its Top Config

Apple has pulled the 512GB unified memory configuration from the M3 Ultra Mac Studio, leaving buyers who need that much local memory with no current path through Apple. The removal appears to have happened sometime in early March 2026, with no announcement. At the same time, the 256GB model jumped $400 in price, and top-RAM configurations are now running four to five months out on delivery, [according to Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/03/apples-512gb-mac-studio-vanishes-a-quiet-acknowledgement-of-the-ram-shortage/)
.

This is a narrow problem. If your workload fits within 128GB, nothing here changes your options. If it doesn't, here's what changed and what the decision looks like right now.

What changed: the Mac Studio 512GB RAM removal and the 256GB price increase
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Apple launched the M3 Ultra Mac Studio on March 1, 2025, with 512GB of unified memory as a headline feature. The specific pitch, [from Apple's March 2025 announcement](https://www.apple.com/in/newsroom/2025/03/apple-unveils-new-mac-studio-the-most-powerful-mac-ever/)
: the machine could run large language models exceeding 600 billion parameters entirely in local memory, no cloud offloading required. Apple called it the most unified memory ever in a personal computer.

That configuration is no longer for sale.

The $9,499 512GB M3 Ultra configuration disappeared from the Apple Store sometime between March 4 and March 6, 2026, without any public notice, as Ars Technica reported when the change became visible. The telling detail is the mismatch: Apple's Tech Specs page still lists the 512GB configuration as an available option, while the Apple Store has removed it entirely. That is not how planned product changes look.

Apple's usual approach when supply tightens is to extend shipping estimates, sometimes by weeks or months, rather than delist the product, per Ars Technica. Pulling a configuration outright is rare behavior. The most straightforward reading is that the company did not expect supply to recover fast enough to keep the option in front of buyers.

The 256GB configuration, now the ceiling across Apple's entire Mac lineup, got more expensive at the same time. Its price climbed from $1,600 to $2,000, a $400 increase with no separate announcement, according to Ars Technica.

The memory architecture across Apple's chip lineup makes that ceiling significant. Ultra chips are the only Apple silicon that can exceed 128GB. The M4 Max and M5 Max both stop at 128GB; Pro chips cap at 64GB; standard M4 and M5 chips top out at 32GB, per Ars Technica. The 256GB Mac Studio is not just the high-end option. It is the only option for any buyer who needs more memory than any other Mac can provide, and it is currently backordered four to five months at $400 more than its launch price.

Why the Mac Studio RAM shortage likely forced Apple to drop the 512GB configuration
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Apple has said nothing publicly, so what follows is inference supported by market conditions and Apple's own earnings disclosures, not confirmed causation.

Memory manufacturers have been shifting production capacity toward high-bandwidth memory, the specialized DRAM used in data center AI accelerators like Nvidia's H200. That reallocation has reduced the available supply of conventional DRAM and driven prices higher across the board. Smaller companies have already responded with repeated price increases and delayed product launches, as Ars Technica documented. Apple, buying at a scale that insulates it longer than most, appears to have absorbed that pressure until it couldn't.

Apple's own earnings call points in the same direction. CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that rising memory costs could begin compressing Apple's profit margins later in 2026, according to Ars Technica. The $400 increase on the 256GB configuration is consistent with real DRAM cost passing through to buyers rather than being absorbed at the margin.

Whether the 512GB removal is temporary or permanent, Apple has not said. The shortage explanation fits the available evidence. It is not confirmed.

Who should buy now, who should wait, and who should look elsewhere
------------------------------------------------------------------

**Need 512GB on a single machine now:** Apple has no option. The configuration is gone from the Apple Store, and there is no announced timeline for its return. The only path that reaches 512GB of pooled Apple memory involves buying two Mac Studios, which costs more than the $9,499 single-system configuration it would nominally replace and introduces interconnect latency that on-die unified memory does not have, per Ars Technica. That tradeoff may be acceptable depending on the workload, but it is not an equivalent substitute.

**Can work within 256GB:** The option exists. Ordering now starts the clock on a four-to-five month delivery window. There is no current basis for expecting the price to fall or availability to open up before that backlog clears, so waiting does not obviously improve the position.

**Can distribute workloads across machines:** macOS Tahoe 26.2 added support for Thunderbolt 5-equipped Macs to operate as a unified compute cluster, allowing distributed compute workloads across systems, according to Ars Technica. Two 256GB Mac Studios could in principle reach 512GB of pooled memory. The tradeoff shows up in three places: the combined cost exceeds the old $9,499 single-system price, interconnect latency adds overhead that a single die avoids, and the cluster feature is still relatively new. Worth tracking as it matures. Not a direct substitute today.

What to watch for
-----------------

The buyer situation as of early April 2026: the 512GB Mac Studio is gone, the 256GB model costs $400 more than it did at launch, and top-RAM configurations are running four to five months out on delivery.

The clearest signal to track is whether Apple restores the 512GB option to the Apple Store, even with an extended ship estimate. That move would confirm a supply disruption rather than a permanent discontinuation. The continued mismatch between Apple's Tech Specs page and its storefront, with no correction in either direction, suggests no resolution is imminent, per Ars Technica.

There is a larger tension underneath the supply problem. Apple spent the past year building a case that large local memory is a decisive advantage for AI work, specifically that a Mac could run very large models locally instead of splitting work across systems or sending it to the cloud. The DRAM market is applying pressure against that premise at exactly the top of the range where it mattered most, as Apple's own 2025 launch materials made clear. Whether this is a temporary supply disruption or something structurally harder to resolve is the question Apple has not answered, and is not, apparently, in a hurry to raise.
